notes.meaning: Paul urges believers to make Christian love their highest and most urgent aim in life. While pursuing love, they should also welcome spiritual gifts given by the Holy Spirit. He especially highlights prophecy because speaking God's message clearly provides the greatest spiritual benefit to the congregation.

differ.view: Prophecy mainly refers to opening and explaining Scripture through preaching, which builds up the congregation.
Prophecy is a continuing spiritual gift where God gives a spontaneous, direct message to encourage and strengthen believers today.

notes.meaning: A person who speaks in an unknown tongue is addressing God in prayer rather than speaking to other people. The people listening cannot understand what is being said. Even though the speaker utters deep spiritual truths by the Holy Spirit, the message does not instruct the room because the words are not understood.

differ.view: In Assemblies of God teaching, speaking in tongues is a genuine gift of prayer and worship directed straight to God. When believers utter "mysteries in the Spirit," the Holy Spirit is helping them pray beyond normal human thinking, which builds up their own inner faith even when others cannot understand them.

In this non-charismatic Baptist reading, tongues were real foreign human languages rather than a private heavenly prayer language. When Paul says the speaker talks only to God and speaks "mysteries," these teachers argue he is not praising the practice, but pointing out that speaking an uninterpreted foreign language in church is useless to human listeners because only God knows what is being said.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Speaking in tongues is genuine spiritual prayer, but its lack of clear meaning to listeners shows why public prophecy is needed to help the church.

notes.meaning: When someone prophesies, they speak God's truth in a language that everyone present can easily understand. This clear message edifies listeners, which means it builds up their faith and helps them grow spiritually. It also offers encouragement to keep serving God and comfort to soothe troubled hearts.

A person who prays in a tongue strengthens his own personal faith and relationship with God. In contrast, someone who prophesies strengthens the whole congregation. Christian gatherings are designed for the common good of everyone present rather than private spiritual benefit.

Paul makes clear that he does not despise tongues and would gladly see all believers receive that gift. Even so, he prefers that they prophesy, because speaking God's message clearly is far more useful to the congregation. A tongue only matches the value of prophecy when someone interprets it so the whole church can be strengthened.

Paul asks how he could possibly help the Corinthian believers if he visited them speaking only in languages they did not know. His visit would only do them good if he brought clear revelation, spiritual knowledge, prophecy, or sound teaching. Words must convey understandable truth to be of any real profit.

Musical instruments like flutes, harps, and military trumpets must produce clear, distinct notes to be understood. If an instrument only plays random, blurry sounds, nobody can tell what song is being played. In the same way, if a battle trumpet does not sound a distinct call, soldiers will not know when to prepare for combat.

In the same way, Christians must speak words in worship that are easy for their listeners to understand. If someone speaks in an uninterpreted language, the words are simply lost in the air. Clear communication is required whenever believers gather to teach and encourage one another.

Every human language across the world carries real meaning to the people who speak it. However, if two people do not know each other's language, they seem like foreigners talking meaningless sounds to one another. Spiritual gifts should never be used in a way that creates that kind of barrier among God's people.

Since the Corinthians are eager to experience spiritual gifts, Paul guides their enthusiasm toward what matters most. He urges them to strive above all for gifts that strengthen and build up the church family. Spiritual excellence is measured by how much a gift helps other people grow in faith.

Anyone who speaks in a tongue should pray for the ability to translate it into the local language. Without interpretation, a person's spirit may pray, but their mind remains unproductive for the rest of the room. Public worship requires both heart devotion and understandable thoughts that others can share.

Paul decides that both the heart and the mind must take part in worship. He resolves to pray and sing with his spirit, while also praying and singing with his mind so everyone can follow along. Genuine Christian worship blends warm spiritual emotion with clear, intelligent understanding.

If someone praises God only in an unknown tongue, ordinary worshippers and newcomers cannot join in the prayer. They cannot even say 'Amen'—a word meaning 'let it be so'—because they do not understand what was said. The individual may be giving thanks well, but the person standing next to them receives no spiritual benefit.

Paul thanks God that he possesses the gift of tongues and uses it more than any of the Corinthians. Yet in a public gathering of the church, he would rather speak five clear words to instruct others than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue. The goal of the church assembly is teaching and helping the body of believers.

Paul urges the believers to stop acting like immature children who are captivated only by flashy novelties. Toward evil and malice they should be as innocent as babies, but in their thinking they need to be mature adults. Grown-up thinking recognizes that spiritual gifts exist to serve others, not for self-display.

Paul quotes the prophet Isaiah to remind them of an Old Testament warning God gave to ancient Israel. Because God's people refused to listen to the clear words of His prophets, He warned that He would speak to them through the foreign speech of invading conquerors. Even hearing those strange foreign tongues would not cause the stubborn people to obey Him.

Paul explains that tongues serve as a sign for unbelievers, whereas prophecy is meant for believers. Just as in the Old Testament, hearing a strange tongue was a sign to an unbelieving people rather than a means of instructing the church. Prophecy, by contrast, conveys God's understandable truth directly to nourish the faith of believers.

differ.view: Tongues serve as a sign of divine judgment and punishment on a rebellious, unbelieving people rather than a sign of grace.
Tongues were given as a miraculous proof of divine power to arrest the attention of unbelievers so they might embrace the gospel.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Tongues serve as an astonishing wonder to confound unbelievers rather than to teach them, while prophecy truly instructs and converts.

notes.meaning: If the whole church gathers and everyone speaks in unknown tongues at once, visiting outsiders and unbelievers will be thoroughly confused. Hearing a room full of people talking in languages nobody understands, they will naturally conclude the worshippers have lost their minds. Such chaos drives seekers away instead of drawing them to Christ.

If an unbeliever enters while believers are prophesying in plain speech, the clear word of God speaks directly to his conscience. The truth reveals the hidden thoughts and sins of his heart, bringing deep spiritual conviction. As a result, he falls on his knees, worships God, and confesses that the Lord is truly present in the congregation.

Early Christian worship was participatory, with different believers arriving ready to offer a psalm, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Paul does not stop their active participation, but he establishes one overarching rule. Everything done in public worship must have the single goal of building up the church.

Paul sets clear boundaries for speaking in tongues in the public gathering. At most two or three people may speak in tongues during a service, they must take turns one by one, and someone must interpret each message. If no interpreter is present, the speaker must stay silent in church and keep his gift for private prayer with God.

Prophecy must also be orderly; only two or three prophets should speak at a single gathering. Meanwhile, the rest of the church leaders and congregation must carefully weigh and evaluate what is said. Every spoken message must be tested to ensure it aligns with God's truth.

If a new revelation comes to someone sitting down, the person currently speaking should quietly yield the floor. In this way, all who have the gift may prophesy one at a time as time allows. Orderly sharing ensures that everyone in the church can be taught and encouraged without shouting or confusion.

Christian prophets are fully able to control their own speech and urges, because the Holy Spirit does not force people into frantic, uncontrollable frenzies. God is a God of peace and harmony, not of noise and disorder. True spiritual gatherings should reflect God's calm character, as seen in all healthy churches.

Paul directs women to remain silent during the public assembly rather than disrupting the service with public debate or teaching. If they have questions about the teaching, they are encouraged to ask their own husbands at home. This instruction aimed to maintain proper order, dignity, and respectful submission in public worship.

differ.view: The Assemblies of God teaches that the Holy Spirit gives speaking and ministry gifts to both men and women, welcoming women to serve as pastors and preachers. They read this passage as a rule for orderly worship that stopped wives from causing disorder by questioning their husbands during the service.

The Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod teaches that God established a lasting order between men and women at creation that still guides the church. They read this passage to mean that women must not lead public worship or carry out the preaching and teaching duties of the pastoral office.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some textual scholars suggest these verses were an early addition made by a later copyist, since some ancient manuscripts place them after verse 40.

notes.meaning: Paul asks the Corinthians whether they imagine the gospel originated with them or was delivered only to their church. His sharp question reminds them that they do not have the right to invent their own disorderly rules. They must conform to the practices followed by the rest of Christ's churches.

Anyone who claims to be a true prophet or truly spiritual must recognize that Paul's instructions are the Lord's own commands, not merely personal advice. If a person stubbornly refuses to accept apostolic authority, he shows his own spiritual blindness and should be disregarded by the church. Genuine spiritual maturity always submits to God's revealed word.

Paul summarizes his entire teaching by urging believers to be eager to prophesy while not forbidding the proper use of tongues. He leaves them with a guiding rule for Christian gatherings: everything must be done in a proper, dignified, and orderly way. Church life flourishes best when freedom of the Spirit is matched with love and order.
